# Splatting
## Overview
Splatting is an object-order volume rendering technique that computes the contribution of each voxel to the image by convolving the voxel with a filter (kernel) that distributes its value to a neighborhood of pixels on the screen [S1, S2]. Unlike ray-casting, which determines how every voxel affects a specific pixel (image-order), splatting determines how every voxel affects every pixel it covers (object-order) [S3, unofficial]. It is distinguished from siblings like [Shear-warp](24-shear-warp.md) and [Texture slicing](25-texture-slicing.md) by its use of continuous, overlapping footprints (splats) rather than discrete slice projections, offering rendering quality similar to ray casting but generally slower than shear-warp [S1].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism of splatting involves treating the volume as a continuous function defined by smooth kernels centered at each voxel [S3, unofficial]. The rendering process follows these shared steps:

1.  **Kernel Definition:** Each voxel is represented by a 3D reconstruction kernel, typically a Gaussian distribution with mean $\mu = 0.0$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 1.0$, truncated outside a radius of $2.0$ with a peak value of $1.0$ [S3, unofficial]. The contribution of a voxel at position $D$ to a screen point $(x,y,z)$ is given by:
    $$ \text{contribution}_D(x,y,z) = h_V(x-D_x, y-D_y, z-D_z) \cdot \rho(D) $$
    where $h_V$ is the volumetric reconstruction kernel and $\rho(D)$ is the voxel density [S3, unofficial].

2.  **Projection (Splatting):** The 3D kernel is projected onto the 2D image plane, creating a "footprint" or "splat" [S1, S2]. The weight of the splat at pixel $(x,y)$ relative to the voxel's projection $(D_x, D_y)$ is:
    $$ \text{weight}(x,y)_D = \text{footprint}(x-D_x, y-D_y) $$
    The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density:
    $$ P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D) $$
    [S3, unofficial].

3.  **Footprint Representation:** For regular grids, the footprint is typically a circle invariant to rotations [S2]. To avoid aliasing, the opacity is convolved with a smoothing kernel (e.g., Gaussian) [S2]. A splat diameter of 1.6 times the spacing between values is sufficient to avoid aliasing while preventing excessive blurring [S2]. For perspective projections, the splat size must be adjusted according to the sample's distance from the viewpoint [S2]. Efficient representation often uses a screen-aligned quadrilateral texture-mapped with an opacity-weighted texture [S2].

4.  **Compositing:** Splats are composited using alpha blending. Depending on the optical model, they must be rendered in front-to-back or back-to-front order [S2]. Compositing in splatting is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time) [S3, unofficial].

5.  **Sheet-Based Traversal:** A common implementation traverses the volume one sheet of voxels at a time, from front to back [S3, unofficial]. The sheet (x-y, x-z, or y-z) nearest to being parallel with the image plane is selected [S3, unofficial]. Each voxel in the sheet is transformed from grid space to screen space, shaded independently to produce an $(R,G,B,\alpha)$ tuple, and projected into an accumulation sheet [S3, unofficial]. The accumulation sheet is composited with the working image after all voxels in the sheet are processed [S3, unofficial].

6.  **Shading:** Shading can be performed via pre-shading (classifying/shading voxels before projection) or post-shading [S3, unofficial]. Post-shading maintains three sheet-buffers (previous, current, next), projects 3D kernels into the next buffer, estimates gradients using central differences on the current buffer based on the next and previous buffers, and shades using the normalized gradient [S3, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Splatting for Anti-aliasing Small Cells](829-splatting-for-anti-aliasing-small-cells.md)
A technique to handle small cells that are missed by slice planes or pixel samples during scan conversion, using splatting to anti-alias and prevent loss of important details in adaptive meshes.

### [Gaussian Splatting](946-gaussian-splatting.md)
Gaussian Splatting is an object-order direct volume rendering algorithm that represents a scene as a collection of overlapping 3D Gaussian primitives, projecting them onto the image plane and alpha-compositing them to generate the final image. It serves as a fast, high-quality alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by leveraging volumetric rendering principles to preserve differentiability while employing point-based rasterization for efficient training and rendering. Unlike traditional opacity-based splatting, 3DGS assigns a single opacity value per primitive, allowing for constant transparency regardless of viewing direction and enabling the optimization of a well-behaved, bounded scalar. It builds on [EWA Splatting](1069-ewa-splatting.md) but simplifies the formulation by ignoring self-attenuation and approximating perspective projection.

### [Ray-Driven Splatting](1156-ray-driven-splatting.md)
A technique merging splatting with raycasting principles, where splats are suspended in object space and rays are spawned to intersect them, enabling perspective projection efficiency and acceleration methods.

### [Footprint Evaluation](1180-footprint-evaluation.md)
A forward mapping rendering algorithm for regular volumetric grids with potentially different spacings in the three grid directions, calculating image plane footprints for each data sample.

### [Single-Pass Splat Rendering Pipeline](1254-single-pass-splat-rendering-pipeline.md)
A rendering pipeline that operates in one single rendering pass, using VBOs for elevation data and texture objects for attributes, avoiding multiple render targets or additional blending passes.

### Early Splat Termination
An optimization for volume splatting that skips processing of voxels when the accumulated opacity at the target screen pixels is already full, analogous to early ray termination in ray casting [S3, unofficial]. It works by projecting two volumes: the density volume and an opacity volume [S3, unofficial]. For each projected voxel, a 2D bounding box is computed around the pixels covering the splat [S3, unofficial]. If all pixels inside the bounding box have full opacity (1.0 or near 1.0), the voxel processing is skipped [S3, unofficial].

### Extinction-based splatting
A rendering solution introduced in [S4] that uses extinction (referred to as 'density' in NeRF literature) instead of the learned opacity value used in 3DGS, to analyze the difference between opacity-based and accurate volumetric rendering. For small numbers of primitives, extinction-based splatting performs better than opacity-based splatting. However, with more primitives, opacity splatting performs best [S4].

### Perspective-Correct Point Splatting Vertex Shader
A vertex shader that renders point clouds as splats (quads or points) with size attenuation based on perspective projection, ensuring the visual size of points corresponds to their world-space radius [S5, unofficial]. It transforms the input position `in_position` to clip space using the `view_proj_matrix` and assigns to `gl_Position` [S5, unofficial]. It calculates `gl_PointSize` using the formula: `viewport_size[1] * (1 / tan(fov_y / 2)) * particle_radius / gl_Position.w`, scaling the point size inversely with depth (`gl_Position.w`) [S5, unofficial]. It passes the `particle_radius` and `in_color` to the fragment shader via the output struct `VertOut` [S5, unofficial]. Parameters include `fov_y` (vertical field of view in radians), `viewport_size` (viewport dimensions, specifically height), and `particle_radius` (world-space radius) [S5, unofficial].

### Splatting Without the Blur
A volume rendering algorithm that performs classification and shading after voxels are projected onto the screen to avoid blurring object edges, which occurs when classification is done prior to projection [S6, unofficial]. It projects voxel densities onto the screen using regular splats (radially symmetric interpolation kernels) [S6, unofficial]. It projects gradient volumes onto the screen using gradient splats, OR computes gradients on the projection plane using central differencing on the projected density [S6, unofficial]. It performs per-pixel shading using the computed gradients to classify and color the voxels [S6, unofficial]. An optimization uses lookup tables for shading to handle the added overhead of screen gradients and per-pixel shading [S6, unofficial]. Computing gradients on the projection plane via central differencing reduces the number of footprint rasterizations by a factor of four compared to projecting a separate gradient volume, because only voxel densities need to be projected [S6, unofficial].

### Hierarchical Splatting
A progressive refinement algorithm for volume rendering using a pyramidal volume representation to achieve real-time interactive rendering [S6, unofficial]. It constructs a pyramidal volume representation that stores average values and estimated error for each cell [S6, unofficial]. It fits an octtree to the pyramid based on a user-supplied precision threshold [S6, unofficial]. It draws the octtree using a set of splats (footprints), where each splat is scaled to match the size of the projection of the corresponding volume cell [S6, unofficial]. It approximates the splats with RGBA Gouraud-shaded polygons for efficient rasterization on modern graphics workstations [S6, unofficial].

### Parallel Splatting
Iterates splats in parallel using `rayon::par_iter().filter_map()` [S7, unofficial]. For each splat, it runs projection and bounding box computation, returning `Some(Projected)` if valid, `None` otherwise [S7, unofficial]. If a `rayon::ThreadPool` is provided, it installs the projection closure into the pool; otherwise, it runs sequentially [S7, unofficial].

### Centralized Conics Approach
A method to compute screen-space position and extents involving the inverse of a 2D-to-2D projective mapping from the splat's parameter space to screen-space [S8, unofficial]. It is an efficient approximation to the exact screen-space position and extents of a splat [S8, unofficial]. However, it is numerically unstable due to large roundoff errors when the projection approaches a line, as the condition number of the mapping increases rapidly [S8, unofficial].

### Splat Radius Adjustment Based on Normal Angle
A method to adjust splat radii to prevent holes between splats when samples are elevated in the normal direction of the base plane, by scaling the radius based on the angle between the splat normal and the base plane normal [S9]. The radius $r$ is calculated as:
$$ r = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu}{0.1 + 0.9\langle n, n_B \rangle} $$
where $r$ is the radius, $\mu$ is the sampling step size of the regular grid, $n$ is the normal vector of the splat, and $n_B$ is the normal vector of the base plane [S9]. The constant 0.1 in the denominator establishes scaling and prevents division by zero or excessively large radii when the dot product is small [S9]. The constant 0.9 in the denominator controls the maximal radius increase; when $\langle n, n_B \rangle = 1$, the denominator is 1.0, and $r = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu$ [S9]. If samples are elevated in the normal direction of the plane, holes may occur between splats if radii are not adjusted [S9]. A large angle between the splat normal and the plane normal indicates large variance between neighboring elevation values, resulting in increased spatial gaps, necessitating larger radii [S9].

### Splat Extent Calculation (Polygon Bounding)
A method to compute screen-space position and extents of a splat by bounding it with a polygon in parameter space, transforming to clip space, clipping against the view-frustum, and performing perspective division [S8, unofficial]. Steps include: 1. Bound the splat by a polygon in its parameter space. 2. Transform the polygon to clip space. 3. Clip the polygon by the view-frustum using the Sutherland-Hodgman algorithm. 4. Perform perspective division on each vertex to yield the clipped polygon in screen-space. 5. Compute desired quantities (position/extents) from the screen-space polygon [S8, unofficial]. The method is not exact but produces a correct upper bound [S8, unofficial].

### MIP-Splatting
An extension that introduces 2D and 3D Gaussian filters to improve robustness to aliasing caused by resolution changes [S10, unofficial].

### GaussianShader
Enriches Gaussians with material parameters such as diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, and normals [S10, unofficial].

### Stop-the-pop
A method that mitigates popping artifacts caused by the sorting procedure in volume splatting [S10, unofficial].

### 3DGUT
A method that employs an unscented transform for more precise Gaussian projection onto the image plane, improving the affine approximation of the projection operator [S10, unofficial].

### SWAG
A method that extends 3DGS by conditioning Gaussians on learned appearance embeddings and training unsupervised transient Gaussians to ignore occluders [S10, unofficial].

### SpotlessSplats
A method that enhances robustness by detecting outliers in a richer, pre-trained feature space to ignore transient distractors [S10, unofficial].

### Gaussian Avatars
A method that trains a FLAME model of the bust, associating each triangle with a Gaussian optimized for the scene but constrained to remain within its corresponding triangle [S10, unofficial].

### Gaussian Avatars
A method that leverages the SMPL model as a prior to reconstruct full-body avatars using pose features to predict Gaussian parameters through a feed-forward network [S10, unofficial].

### 3DGS-Avatar
A method that reconstructs full-body avatars by combining Gaussians with both non-rigid and rigid transformations of an underlying SMPL model [S10, unofficial].

### Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars
A method that introduces relightable Gaussian avatars, supporting more diverse lighting conditions [S10, unofficial].

### PixelSplat
A method that incorporates an epipolar transformer to generalize features between two views, paired with a probabilistic prediction of Gaussians aligned along camera-to-pixel rays [S10, unofficial].

### MAtCha
A method that employs an atlas-of-charts and depth estimation as input to an MLP, which deforms the atlas and produces high-quality meshes represented with 2D Gaussians [S10, unofficial].

## Background
Splatting was originally proposed by Lee Westover in 1990 [S3, unofficial]. It is based on the idea of treating each voxel as a fuzzy spherical ball (3D Gaussian) projected onto the screen, determining how every pixel might be affected by that voxel, as opposed to ray-casting which determines how every voxel affects a pixel [S3, unofficial]. The continuous volume is defined as a collection of smooth functions (Gaussians) centered at each voxel, with density assigned at the center and dropping off according to the distribution [S3, unofficial]. The term "splat" refers to the footprint left on the image plane, analogous to throwing a cube of gelatinous material onto the plane [S1].

Axis-aligned sheet buffered splatting causes 'popping' artifacts when viewing angles change around 45 degrees because kernels in consecutive sheets are composited together while kernels on the same sheet are added together, and addition/compositing are not equivalent [S3, unofficial]. To mitigate this, image-aligned sheet buffered splatting aligns sheet buffers parallel with the image plane regardless of volume orientation, slicing the volume into thin slabs representing portions of the line integral through the entire kernel [S3, unofficial].

Splatting algorithms suffer from time-consuming computations necessary to compute the view-dependent filters with which to convolute the voxels in the volume [S1]. Observations showed that overall splatting offers a rendering quality similar to that of ray casting, and both ray casting and splatting provided in some cases better image qualities than shear-warp [S1]. This is because in shear-warp, rendered voxels were interpolated without prior opacity and color being incorporated, whereas splatting incorporates these during the footprint projection [S1].
